findings.title: Public findMany method removed without updating consumers
findings.body: This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from `InsightsBookingService` and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The diff updates only this service and its tests; no other call sites are migrated. Any code that invokes `service.findMany({...})` will fail to compile (method no longer exists), and any caller that relied on the previous behavior (merging caller-supplied `where`/`select`/pagination with the authorization and filter conditions) must now build and execute its own `$queryRaw`. If such consumers exist, this is a breaking change that is not covered by the PR.

findings.title: Only user-scope conditions are actually executed against the database
findings.body: The single test that runs the generated SQL (`prisma.$queryRaw ... WHERE ${baseConditions}`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose authorization condition contains no array parameter. The security-critical org/team paths, which build `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})`, are only checked structurally via `toEqual(Prisma.sql...)` and never executed. Prisma array binding into `ANY($1)` has known type-inference pitfalls (e.g. requiring a cast such as `::int[]`, or failing when the array is empty). A broken/empty array binding would therefore pass this suite but throw or silently return no rows in production, which is precisely the parameter-binding risk the PR description flags.

findings.title: Org-scope assertion depends on DB row ordering of team/user IDs
findings.body: The org-scope test compares the service's `Prisma.Sql` to a literal with `teamIds` ordered `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `userIds` ordered `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. The service builds those arrays from `teamRepo.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, neither of which is shown to enforce an `ORDER BY`. `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` compares the interpolated value arrays element-by-element, so if Postgres returns the rows in a different order the arrays differ and the test fails even though the generated SQL is semantically identical (`ANY(...)` is order-insensitive). This makes the test flaky/order-dependent rather than validating behavior; either sort the arrays before comparison or assert the query result instead.

findings.title: getFilterConditions can return an unparenthesized OR fragment
findings.body: For an `eventTypeId` filter, `buildFilterConditions` pushes `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` and, when it is the only filter, returns that fragment without an outer grouping (and the test at line 385 asserts this unparenthesized form). `getBaseConditions` compensates by wrapping it in parentheses, but `getFilterConditions` is a public method returning a bare `Prisma.Sql`; any other consumer that embeds it next to another `AND`/`OR` in a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE ${getFilterConditions()} AND ...`) would hit operator-precedence and match too many rows. Consider always returning a fully parenthesized fragment so the method is safe to compose.

findings.title: Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains
findings.body: The PR deletes the entire "Caching" describe block (the `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions` tests), but the service still caches results via `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` in `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`. The caching paths are now untested, so a regression in cache-keying or cache invalidation would go unnoticed.
